en: I. In the city of [Name], there was a son of the king named Śrīmañjuvarman, who had performed services for previous Victors, had attained the roots of virtue conducive to liberation, possessed the true lineage of the Mahāyāna, and was skilled in all arts. At the time of his consecration as crown prince, while he was being heated by hot water poured by his mother, the queen—who was an emanation of a vajra-woman—he was unable to endure the heat and was addressed [by her].

"O son, three do not go to heaven: a king, a painter, and a poet. Having become a lord of men and committed evil, when you die and go to hell, your suffering will be even more intense than this; enough with this kingdom! Go, my child, to the land of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—the realm of Śrī Mañjuvajra—and it will be well for you."

III. Therefore, placing his mother’s command upon his head, he set out with an unswerving heart, mounted upon his excellent bay horse. Traveling incessantly for many days, without regard for food, drink, or other necessities, his mind single-pointedly fixed on her instruction, he beheld a jewel of a maiden in a certain forest; she dismounted him from the horse by holding it steady.

IV. Afflicted by thirst, he saw water and prepared to drink; she stopped him, saying, "This is poisonous water," and made him drink other water that was nectar, and having burned meat with fire, she fed him. V. Once restored to health, he said to her, "From where have you come? She replied, "Our guru, the glorious Mañjuvajra—who is established in meditative absorption, whose marketplace is great compassion, and who is adorned with a multitude of excellent qualities—resides here. I have come from his presence. Having been told this, like a person who has found a jewel, the suffering man attained supreme joy.

VI. Having said, "Show him that very [person]," he was received by her; taking the horse, he went and beheld the Guru—who was the receptacle of a multitude of heavy virtues, steadfast and profound, and who had attained tranquility, self-restraint, and asceticism. Having saluted both the horse and himself before the Guru, he requested of the Guru: "By granting me instruction regarding the eternal and the non-eternal, deliver me from this ocean of endless and terrible suffering..."

VII. Having been instructed by him according to the sequence of transmission, he remained there for twelve years practicing concentration. Having directly perceived Mañjuvajra and attained the wisdom of Mañjuśrī, he was commanded by his guru, "Go to the Middle Country. Having gone there, he served the King of Magadha. Serving as a *rāuta* (or *rāuṭa*), named Acalasena, he dwelt in the garden of Dharma with the conduct of a *rāuta*, possessing a sword made of *devadāru* wood kept within his treasury.

VIII. After some time, other royal servants (*rāuta*), unable to endure his success, petitioned the king: "Your Majesty, since Acala serves with the Devadāru sword, how will he fight at the time of battle? Therefore, Your Majesty, please examine his sword. Thinking, "He is invincible and cannot be commanded," their vital points were tormented by the thorn of envy; thus, having gathered together, they requested under the pretext of a royal command that the swords of all be inspected. Having looked at the sabers of everyone, the inspection of Acala’s sword was carried out.

IX. Acala-sena said, "It is not fitting for me to show my sword, even though you have thrice forbidden [me], because I am steadfast [in my resolve] (variant: because of my persistence), O King. Close one eye and look at it. When this was shown to him in a secluded place, one of the king's eyes fell to the ground due to the blaze of that sword. Reflecting upon the king who had been won over by the sight of its power, he placed [the eye] upon a polished stone slab, extinguished it (variant:
healed the wound), went to the great monastery of Śrī Nālandā, and renounced the world under another guise.

X. Because of his extreme tranquility, the one named Śāntideva meditated after hearing the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka). Even while eating, even while sleeping, and even when gone to his hut, he remained in that very state; because he had attained the samādhi of Bhusuku, he became known by the name Bhusuku.

XI. Within the Saṅgha as well, after some time, certain foolish and curious individuals deliberated: "Let it first be examined whether this man knows anything or not. There, every year in the month of Jyeṣṭha during the bright fortnight, Pūraṇa and others—who had previously been refuted by the Teacher through displays of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*)—would perform recitations in imitation of him; it was there that he was to be examined. Thus instructed, he replied again and again, "I know nothing," until he was finally commanded: "Speak!"

Outside the monastery, in a spacious Dharma-hall situated to the northeast, he himself reflected in the midst of a circle of great scholars: "I have three works previously composed—the *Sūtrasamuccaya*, the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, and the treatise called the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*. Having kept this in mind, he ascended the lion throne and said: "Which shall I recite: the words of the Sage (*ārṣa*) or their meaning (*arthārṣa*)?"

XIII. In this context, a *ṛṣi* is one who possesses knowledge of the ultimate truth; [the word] is derived from the root *ṛṣ* (to go) with the suffix *kvin* according to the *Uṇādi* rules. That which was spoken by the *ṛṣi*, the Victor (*jina*), is called *ārṣa*. Now, if one asks: "How can that which was taught by Subhūti and others in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras be considered *ārṣa*?"—it is said in response to this that it was [actually] taught by the Crown Prince, the noble Maitreya.
That speech which is meaningful, endowed with the foundations of dharma, which eradicates the afflictions of the three realms,
and which demonstrates the benefits of peace— [that alone is the word of the Buddha].
Thus it has been said: "The word of the Ṛṣis is authoritative; otherwise, it is the opposite."

XIV. That which was drawn forth by the noble ones and others is the word of the Sage; however, the teaching of Subhūti and others is due to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Blessed One, and thus there is no fault.
XV. Out of curiosity, they said, "Let that which is the very word of the Sage be recited first," and he began to recite the *Caryāvatāra*. In that recitation:
"When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind, then, due to the absence of any other alternative, it becomes supportless and is stilled."
Thus, in this verse, the Blessed Mañjuśrī appeared before him; he, together with that very [Mañjuśrī], went into the sky and gradually vanished.

XVI. Then, after Bhadradarśana had become disillusioned [with worldly life], while searching through his cell, the three books beginning with the *Sūtrasamuccaya* were found in a small wooden hut; these were subsequently circulated in the world by scholars. Regarding this, there is the verse beginning with "The Sugata... [This book was written by the monk Śrīkīrti Paṇḍita of Kāṣṭhamaṇḍapa].
